title: Choosing a Concurrency Architecture
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of choosing a concurrency architecture in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply choosing a concurrency architecture in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to measuring benefits before introducing complexity and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Choosing a Concurrency Architecture through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding choosing a concurrency architecture helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Choosing a Concurrency Architecture helps you reason about threads versus processes versus ractors. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Threads versus processes versus Ractors. Then connect it to Fibers and asynchronous I/O. The remaining syllabus points—Communication overhead, Measuring benefits before introducing complexity—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Choosing a Concurrency Architecture
content_blocks.code:
queue = Queue.new
worker = Thread.new { queue << "finished" }
puts queue.pop
worker.join

items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Treating an example as a universal rule
items.text: Check Ruby version, runtime implementation, and third-party library documentation when behavior is version-sensitive.

items.text: Separate input parsing, domain behavior, and output so each piece is easier to test.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports choosing a concurrency architecture. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for choosing a concurrency architecture using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Measuring benefits before introducing complexity), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain choosing a concurrency architecture, identify its place in concurrency and asynchronous programming, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
